text.p: Oceans are threatened by pollution, over-fishing and transport of dangerous substances including plutonium, the Independent World Commission on the Oceans warned on Friday.

The 43-member commission, launched last December to gather scientific evidence on the state of oceans, is to present its final report to the U.N. General Assembly in 1998 -- designated international year of the oceans.

"The commission's purpose is to sound the alarm to the world community because this problem doesn't simply concern those living by the sea," chairman Mario Soares, the former Portuguese president, told a news conference.

"The seas belong to everyone -- not certain powers that possess technical know-how to exploit what exists," he said. "We don't need new laws or legislation. What we have to do is see that existing legislation is implemented and enforced."
The U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, which regulates mining of the deep sea bed, entered into force in 1994 and has been ratified by 107 countries.
More than 150 million people worldwide earn a living from fishing.

However, in six of the 11 major fishing regions of the world, more than 60 per cent of commercial fish stocks have either been depleted or are currently being fished to their limits, according to the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation.

Former Costa Rican president and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oscar Arias, former Dutch prime minister Ruud Lubbers, and U.S. congressman Patrick Kennedy (Rhode Island) are among the members of the commission, which next meets in Rotterdam in November.
